A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same learning-rate scaling study. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial reorganization and some inconsistent experiment labels.

before.justification: V1 reports original RefinedWeb language-model training experiments, validation losses, fitted optimal learning rates, and bootstrap and multiple-seed analyses.

after.justification: V3 retains these original experiments and adds architecture-transfer, repeated-token, held-out validation, and statistical results.

M1.justification: The quadratic-fitting and power-law approach remains. However, the practical transfer formula changes from exponent +0.34 in v1 Equation (10) to -0.32 in v3 Equation (5), correcting its direction. V3 Section 6 also introduces a depth-and-horizon transfer recipe combined with muP-style width transfer.

E1.justification: Both versions study next-token language modeling on RefinedWeb. The added small Llama model and repeated-token experiments vary architecture, subset size, and training procedures within this retained dataset and task; they introduce no additional data domain or task.

E2.justification: The comparison methods remain empirical LR optima, scaling-law predictions, unchanged-LR transfer, and the LR used by Llama-1. MuP remains a tested parameterization. Newly discussed related methods are not added as evaluated competitors.

E3.justification: V1 Figure 7 presents a joint fit spanning 350M through 7B models without separate validation. V3 Section 4 fits the 760M, 1.3B, and 2.7B models and explicitly withholds 7B for validation. New protocols also test a 50M Llama architecture and one, two, or four epochs over a fixed 25B-token subset. These materially extend the evaluation design.

E4.justification: V3 adds direct tests of whether the scaling exponent transfers between architectures (Figure 11) and whether token reuse changes the scaling relationship (Figure 12). These address generalization and a confound left unresolved in v1. Section 4.1 also adds an estimated Llama-1 loss-penalty analysis; the existing batch-size and muP analyses are retained.

E5.justification: V3 consistently states 1000 bootstrap repetitions, replacing v1's conflicting counts of 10 in the text and 100 in Table 4's caption. It also reports bootstrap uncertainty for R² and beta in Table 10. The three-seed results are unchanged; 'two additional seeds' clarifies v1's wording rather than establishing more independent training repetitions.

E6.justification: V3 adds architecture-transfer and repeated-token findings, per-model beta values, 125M extrapolation results, bootstrap fit statistics, held-out 7B R² of 0.978, and a claimed loss penalty of 0.027. These substantially expand the reported evidence. Table 1's numerical entries and the three-seed losses remain unchanged; its conflicting model labels are standardized to 50M, so the new 125M table should not be interpreted as a matched performance change.

T1.justification: The joint power-law derivation in v1 Section 4.2 is retained in v3 Appendix C, rather than newly introduced. Mathematical changes include correcting the practical transfer formula and using N proportional to layer count times squared width to motivate the new depth-transfer expression. No substantial new proof framework appears.

C1.justification: The three central contributions remain: horizon-dependent optimal LR, power-law transfer, and evidence that Llama-1 used an excessive LR. V3 removes the abstract's explicit claim to estimate the resulting performance hit and softens the introduction's description of horizon transfer from unstudied to understudied. The overall research claim remains stable.

C2.justification: V1 leaves fresh versus repeated tokens unresolved; v3 interprets Figure 12 as evidence that total training tokens govern the scaling. V3 also explicitly limits the joint law to models of at least 760M parameters, replacing advice beginning at 350M, and adds interpretations concerning architecture transfer and an extrapolated Llama loss-penalty upper bound. These materially revise applicability and interpretation.

D1.justification: V3 discloses more than 250 training runs, states that polynomial fits have more observations than free parameters, and identifies the divergent runs as those using the highest LR. It also reconciles the muP experiment's textual model size with the existing 50M figure label. Appendix A's architecture and hyperparameter tables and the stated Megatron codebase remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V3 substantially elaborates its comparison with the already-cited Everett et al., discussing fixed-horizon assumptions and differing conclusions about scaling exponents. It adds Wang and Aitchison on AdamW weight decay and removes references including Tissue, Henighan, Abdin, and Huber. These refine the existing positioning around scaling laws and hyperparameter transfer.

P1.justification: V3 extensively edits and clarifies the prose and reorganizes the narrative. MuP, variance, and batch-size analyses move into Section 3; joint model-size scaling receives a dedicated Section 4; its derivation moves to Appendix C. Experimental setup, related work, limitations, and practitioner advice are substantially rewritten, beyond simply inserting new results.

P2.justification: V3 adds missing horizon legends, standardizes plot colors, redraws the joint-fit display to identify held-out data, and adds an annotated Llama extrapolation plot. New architecture and repeated-token figures and additional statistical tables expand the displays. Several existing figures and tables move to the appendix, while the coefficient table becomes an equation.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially improves practical reliability and empirical support by correcting the LR-transfer formula, adding explicit held-out validation of the joint law, and testing architecture transfer and the token-reuse question left open in v1. Clearer applicability limits and figure legends also improve usability. The gains are tempered by errors in new material: the positive 0.027 penalty is written with reversed subtraction, and Table 10 describes a 2.03% relative deviation as roughly 10%. These localized problems do not outweigh the stronger validation and corrected guidance.
